title: Egeria. Hippolytus
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Furnished with such teachings and others like them, Numa returns to his own country, is sought out unasked to take the reins of the Latian people, teaches the rites of sacrifice, and turns a nation bred to savage war to the arts of peace before dying old; his widow then hides in the woods of the Arician valley and breaks in on Diana's rites with her mourning. Hippolytus, the son of Theseus, tries to quiet her by telling his own death — his stepmother's false charge, his father's curse and exile, a bull out of the sea, and his body torn to pieces in the harness — and his restoration by Apollo's offspring, after which Diana hid him in this grove under the name Virbius. Egeria is not consoled, and the goddess at last dissolves her body into a cold spring.
advisory: This part stops to describe Hippolytus's body being torn apart after he is thrown from his chariot and held fast by the harness straps — living entrails, sinews, limbs and broken bones itemised over six lines — and Lectorium presents the text unaltered.

sentences.t:
Talibus atque aliis instructum pectora dictis
in patriam remeasse ferunt ultroque petitum
accepisse Numam populi Latiaris habenas.
sentences.l: Furnished as to his breast with such sayings and others, Numa, they report, went back to his fatherland and, sought out unasked, took up the reins of the Latian people.
sentences.i: Furnished in mind with such teachings and others like them, Numa, they say, returned to his own country, and when he was sought out unasked, he took up the reins of the Latian people.
sentences.n: *ferunt*, “they report”, governs the two perfect infinitives *remeasse* (a syncopated *remeavisse*) and *accepisse*, with *Numam* as their accusative subject. *pectora* is a Greek accusative of respect after the participle *instructum* — “equipped as to his breast” — and the literal keeps it, the idiomatic turns it into “in mind”. *ultro* is “unbidden, of their own accord”, and *petitum* agrees with *Numam*: the people came to him. Magnus prints *instructum pectora*; some editions print *instructo pectore*, an ablative, which removes the Greek accusative altogether.

sentences.t:
Coniuge qui felix nympha ducibusque Camenis
sacrificos docuit ritus gentemque feroci
adsuetam bello pacis traduxit ad artes.
sentences.l: And he, blessed in a nymph for wife and in the Camenae for guides, taught the rites of sacrifice, and a nation accustomed to savage war he brought over to the arts of peace.
sentences.i: Blessed in his nymph-wife and in the Camenae for guides, he taught the rites of sacrifice and led a people bred to savage war over into the arts of peace.
sentences.n: *qui* opens the sentence as a connecting relative — “and he”, not “who”; it does the same at 485, and *quam* does it at 534. *coniuge ... nympha* and *ducibus ... Camenis* are ablatives with *felix*, “fortunate in”. The Camenae are the Italian goddesses of springs and song. *feroci* closes 483 and *bello*, the noun it agrees with, stands second in 484, so the adjective reaches across the line-end to it. *traduxit ad* is “led across to”, a verb of bringing a whole people over from one condition to another.

sentences.l: And when he, now an old man, had run out both his reign and his lifetime, the Latian young wives and the people and the fathers wept for Numa dead;
sentences.i: And when he had grown old and finished both his reign and his life, the young wives of Latium, the people and the senators all wept for Numa dead;
sentences.n: *deflevere* is *defleverunt*: the poetic third-plural perfect in *-ēre*, which recurs at *monuere* in 491 — flagged here and only nudged there. *qui* is again the connecting relative, “and he”. *senior* is the comparative of *senex* used predicatively, literally “the older man”, so “now an old man”. The triple *-que ... -que ... -que* piles the three groups of mourners together; *patres* are the senators, and *nurus* the young married women. *exstinctum* agrees with *Numam*, held back to the end of the clause.

sentences.t:
nam coniunx urbe relicta
vallis Aricinae densis latet abdita silvis
sacraque Oresteae gemitu questuque Dianae
impedit:
sentences.l: for his wife, the city left behind, lies hidden, buried away in the dense woods of the Arician valley, and with groaning and lamenting obstructs the rites of Orestean Diana:
sentences.i: for his wife has left the city and lies hidden away in the thick woods of the valley of Aricia, and her groaning and lamenting break in upon the rites of Orestean Diana:
sentences.n: *urbe relicta* is an ablative absolute — a self-contained “with the city left behind” where English wants a clause; the literal keeps the participial shape, the idiomatic breaks it out. *latet* and *impedit* are present tenses inside a past narrative, the historic present that keeps the scene running. *abdita* is a second participle stacked on *latet*, “hidden, buried”. *Oresteae* is an epithet of the Diana worshipped at Aricia; these lines do not explain it. The wife is not named until 547.

sentences.t:
a! quotiens nymphae nemorisque lacusque,
ne faceret, monuere et consolantia verba
dixerunt.
sentences.l: Ah! how often did the nymphs of the grove and of the lake warn her not to do it, and speak consoling words.
sentences.i: Ah, how often the nymphs of the grove and the lake warned her against it and spoke words of comfort!
sentences.n: *monuere* = *monuerunt*, the *-ēre* perfect again. *ne faceret* is the negative indirect command after *monuere*, imperfect subjunctive in secondary sequence, with the thing not to be done left unexpressed — “not to do it”. *a!* is an exclamation in the poet's own voice, breaking into the narrative. *quotiens* is picked up again at the opening of the next sentence in 492.

sentences.l: How often to her as she wept did the hero, the son of Theseus, say “Set a limit!” — “for it is not your fortune alone that must be lamented;
sentences.i: How often did the Thesean hero say to her as she wept, “Put a limit to it! It is not your fortune alone that deserves lamenting;
sentences.n: *flenti* is a participle used as a noun in the dative, “to her weeping”. *Theseius heros*, “the Thesean hero”, names the speaker only by his father; he gives his own name at 497 and claims it at 500. *querenda* is a gerundive of obligation with *est*, “must be lamented”. The archived edition prints *ne que* here as two separate words where the sense requires the single *neque*, “and not”; other editions print *neque*. It is left exactly as printed.

sentences.t: similes aliorum respice casus:
sentences.l: look upon the like misfortunes of others:
sentences.i: look at the misfortunes of others, which are like your own:
sentences.n: *respice* is the imperative, “look back at, consider”. *similes* and *casus* are the two ends of one accusative phrase, with *aliorum* and the verb standing inside them — a piece of interlocking word order that English cannot copy, so the literal restores the pieces to each other.

sentences.t:
mitius ista feres, utinamque exempla dolentem
non mea te possent relevare!
sentences.l: more gently will you bear these things — and would that examples not my own could relieve you in your grief!
sentences.i: You will bear it more gently then — and I wish it were examples other than mine that could ease your grief!
sentences.n: *utinam* with the imperfect subjunctive *possent* is a wish for the present that is not being fulfilled: the examples that could console her are, unfortunately, his own. *dolentem* is a participle agreeing with *te*, “you grieving”. *exempla* stands in 495 and the *non mea* that qualifies it opens 496, so the negative lands only after the noun. *mitius* is the comparative adverb.

sentences.t: Sed et mea possunt.
sentences.l: But mine also can.
sentences.i: But mine can, too.
sentences.n: The subject of *possunt* is *exempla* carried over from the sentence before, and *relevare* is likewise understood: “but my examples can relieve you”. *et* here is “also, too”, not “and”.

sentences.t:
Fando aliquem Hippolytum vestras puto, contigit aures
credulitate patris, sceleratae fraude novercae
occubuisse neci:
sentences.l: By the telling of it — I think — it has touched your ears that a certain Hippolytus met his death through his father's credulity, through the trickery of a criminal stepmother:
sentences.i: By report, I suppose, it has come to your ears that a certain Hippolytus met his death through his father's credulity and the trickery of a criminal stepmother:
sentences.n: *fando* is an ablative of the gerund, “by speaking”, so “by report”. *puto*, “I think”, sits parenthetically inside the clause. The subject of *contigit ... aures* is the whole accusative-and-infinitive *aliquem Hippolytum ... occubuisse*; *neci* is the dative with *occubuisse*, “fell to death”. *sceleratae* is Hippolytus's own word for her — “criminal, guilt-laden” — and both layers keep it at that force. Magnus prints *puto*; some editions print *si*, which turns the statement into a condition, “if by report ...”.

sentences.t:
mirabere, vixque probabo,
sed tamen ille ego sum.
sentences.l: you will wonder, and I shall scarcely prove it, but nevertheless I am he.
sentences.i: You will be amazed, and I shall hardly prove it — but all the same, I am he.
sentences.n: *mirabere* is *miraberis*, the alternative second-singular future ending in *-re* for *-ris*. *ille ego sum* — “that man, I am he” — points back to the *aliquem Hippolytum* of 497, which is why the literal keeps the bare “he” rather than repeating the name.

sentences.t:
Me Pasiphaeia quondam
temptatum frustra patrium temerare cubile,
quod voluit, voluisse,
sentences.l: That I — on whom Pasiphaë's daughter once made an attempt in vain, that I might defile my father's bed — had wanted what she wanted,
sentences.i: That I had wanted what she wanted — I, on whom Pasiphaë's daughter once made an attempt in vain, to get me to defile my father's bed —
sentences.n: *Me* is the accusative subject of the infinitive *voluisse*, and *temptatum* is a participle agreeing with it: “me, having been made an attempt on”. *temerare* is the infinitive of the thing she attempted to bring about. The verb that governs this whole accusative-and-infinitive, *damnavit*, does not arrive until 504, so the unit is left suspended. *Pasiphaeia*, “Pasiphaë's daughter”, is the only name she is given anywhere in these lines.

sentences.t:
infelix crimine verso
(indiciine metu magis offensane repulsae?)
damnavit, meritumque nihil pater eicit urbe
hostilique caput prece detestatur euntis.
sentences.l: the ill-fated woman, with the charge turned round (from fear of denunciation the more, or offended at the rebuff?), condemned me; and my father, though I had deserved nothing of it, casts me out of the city, and with a hostile prayer curses the head of me as I go.
sentences.i: the ill-fated woman turned the charge about and condemned me — was it more from fear of being denounced, or was she stung by refusal? — and my father, though I had done nothing to deserve it, drives me out of the city and with a hostile prayer calls down a curse on my head as I go.
sentences.n: The object of *damnavit* is the *Me* back at 500. *crimine verso* is an ablative absolute, “the charge having been turned round”: the accusation she brought was the one that lay against her. The doubled *-ne ... -ne* in 503 sets two possible motives side by side as a question Hippolytus asks in his own voice and does not answer. *meritum nihil* agrees with an unexpressed “me”, with *nihil* as its internal accusative — “having deserved nothing of it”, which is what the literal renders; *euntis* is a genitive agreeing with an understood *mei*, “of me as I go”. The perfect *damnavit* gives way to the presents *eicit* and *detestatur* — the historic present again, quickening the expulsion. Magnus prints *infelix* here; some editions print *et* and add *finxit* in this sentence.

sentences.t:
Pittheam profugo curru Troezena petebam,
iamque Corinthiaci carpebam litora ponti,
sentences.l: I was making for Pittheus's Troezen in a fugitive chariot, and already I was skirting the shores of the Corinthian sea,
sentences.i: I was heading for Troezen, Pittheus's city, in flight in my chariot, and already I was making my way along the shore of the Corinthian gulf,
sentences.n: *Troezena* is a Greek accusative singular, and *Pittheam* the adjective from Pittheus. *carpere litora* is literally “to crop the shores”, used of steadily eating up ground along them. The two imperfects *petebam* and *carpebam* hold the scene open for the *cum*-clause that follows immediately.

sentences.t:
cum mare surrexit, cumulusque inmanis aquarum
in montis speciem curvari et crescere visus
et dare mugitus summoque cacumine findi.
sentences.l: when the sea rose up, and a monstrous heap of waters seemed to curve into the shape of a mountain and to grow, and to give out bellowings, and to be split at its topmost peak.
sentences.i: when the sea rose, and a monstrous mass of water seemed to arch into the shape of a mountain and swell, and to bellow, and to split at its very summit.
sentences.n: This is an inverted *cum*: the grammatically subordinate clause carries the event the sentence exists for, while the main verbs before it were only the setting. *visus* stands for *visus est*, the copula omitted, and it governs four infinitives in a row — *curvari*, *crescere*, *dare*, *findi* — which the literal keeps as four. *inmanis* is the edition's spelling and is kept.

sentences.t:
Corniger hinc taurus ruptis expellitur undis,
pectoribusque tenus molles erectus in auras
naribus et patulo partem maris evomit ore.
sentences.l: From there a horned bull is driven out, the waves being burst, and, reared breast-high into the yielding air, he spews out part of the sea from his nostrils and his gaping mouth.
sentences.i: The waves burst apart, and out of them a horned bull is thrust forth, and, reared up breast-high into the soft air, he spews part of the sea from his nostrils and his wide-open mouth.
sentences.n: *ruptis ... undis* is another ablative absolute, “the waves having been burst”. *tenus* is a postposition and follows the ablative it governs, *pectoribus tenus*, “as far as the breast”. *erectus* is a perfect passive participle used of the bull's own rearing, where English wants an active. *corniger*, “horn-bearing”, is a compound adjective.

sentences.t: Corda pavent comitum.
sentences.l: The hearts of my companions quake.
sentences.i: My companions' hearts quail.
sentences.n: *corda*, “hearts”, is a neuter plural subject with the plural verb *pavent*. The present tense continues the run of historic presents begun at *expellitur* in 511 and *evomit* in 513.

sentences.t:
Mihi mens interrita mansit
exsiliis contenta suis:
sentences.l: For me my mind remained undismayed, content with its own banishments:
sentences.i: My own mind stayed unshaken, content with its exile:
sentences.n: *mihi* is a dative of reference, “for me, in my case”, set against the companions of the clause just before it, which stands in the same line, 514. *interrita*, “not terrified”, and *contenta* are both predicative with *mens*, and *contenta* takes the ablative *exsiliis*. *exsiliis* is plural where one exile is meant — a poetic plural the literal keeps and the idiomatic quietly resolves.

sentences.t:
cum colla feroces
ad freta convertunt adrectisque auribus horrent
quadrupedes monstrique metu turbantur et altis
praecipitant currum scopulis;
sentences.l: when my fierce four-footed team turn their necks toward the straits and bristle with ears pricked up, and are thrown into confusion by fear of the monster, and hurl the chariot headlong from the high crags;
sentences.i: when my wild team swing their necks round toward the sea, bristle with their ears pricked, panic in terror at the monster, and pitch the chariot down the high crags;
sentences.n: A second inverted *cum*, like the one at 508, though its verbs are present where 508 had the perfect *surrexit*. *feroces* closes 515 and the noun it agrees with, *quadrupedes*, opens 517, with a whole line standing between them. *quadrupedes*, “four-footed ones”, is here the word for the horses. *adrectis auribus* is an ablative absolute again. *altis ... scopulis* is an ablative taken here as separation, “from the high crags”; it could also be read as the place they dash the chariot upon.

sentences.t:
ego ducere vana
frena manu spumis albentibus oblita luctor
et retro lentas tendo resupinus habenas.
sentences.l: I struggle to guide with useless hand the bit smeared with whitening foam, and, bent back, I pull the tough reins backwards.
sentences.i: I fight to hold the foam-smeared bit in a hand that can do nothing, and, thrown back on my shoulders, I haul the tough reins in.
sentences.n: *luctor* takes the infinitive *ducere*, “I struggle to guide”. *oblita* is from *oblino*, “smear”, and agrees with *frena* — not from *obliviscor*, “forget”, which it looks exactly like. *vana ... manu* moves the uselessness onto the hand itself. *resupinus*, “bent back”, is an adjective where English wants a phrase, and the idiomatic spells it out as “thrown back on my shoulders”. *frena* in 519 is the bit and bridle and *habenas* in 520 the reins, and the Latin keeps them distinct.

sentences.t: Nec vires tamen has rabies superasset equorum.
sentences.l: And yet the horses' madness would not have overcome this strength of mine.
sentences.i: Even so, the horses' frenzy would not have beaten my strength.
sentences.n: *superasset* = *superavisset*, a pluperfect subjunctive: this is the apodosis of a past condition contrary to fact, and its *ni*-clause follows in the next unit. The archived edition prints a full stop after *equorum* and then a lower-case *ni*, so it breaks a single sentence in two. Counting the other places in this part where a full stop, a question mark or an exclamation mark ends a sentence: sixteen of them are followed by a capital and none by a lower-case letter. The edition does print a lower-case letter after such a mark where the mark stands inside a sentence — after the interjection *a!* at 490, after the exclamation inside the speech at 493, and after the closed parenthesis at 503 — but the stop at 521 is the only full stop anywhere in the part that is followed by a lower-case letter. The punctuation and the lower-case letter are shipped exactly as printed and the unit division follows them.

sentences.t:
ni rota, perpetuum qua circumvertitur axem,
stipitis occursu fracta ac disiecta fuisset.
sentences.l: had not the wheel, where it is turned about the unbroken axle, been broken and flung apart by the impact of a stump.
sentences.i: if the wheel, at the point where it turns about its unbroken axle, had not struck a stump and been shattered and flung apart.
sentences.n: *ni* is *nisi*, “if not”: this clause completes the condition whose main half stands in the unit before, across the edition's full stop. *fracta ac disiecta fuisset* uses *fuisset* where prose would more often have *esset*. *stipitis occursu* is an ablative of means, “by the encounter with a stump”; the same stump returns at 525 as *in stipe*. *perpetuum ... axem* is an accusative with the middle-passive *circumvertitur*; the construction is compressed, and “turns about the unbroken axle” is the sense taken here.

sentences.t:
Excutior curru, lorisque tenentibus artus
viscera viva trahi nervosque in stipe teneri,
membra rapi partim, partim reprensa relinqui,
sentences.l: I am shaken out of the chariot, and, the straps holding my limbs, [you would see] my living entrails dragged along and my sinews held fast on the stump, my limbs snatched away in part, in part caught and left behind,
sentences.i: I am flung out of the chariot, and, with the straps holding my limbs fast, you would see my living entrails dragged along and my sinews caught on the stump, my limbs part torn away, part snagged and left behind,
sentences.n: *excutior* is passive and present, keeping the historic present through the catastrophe. *loris tenentibus artus* is an ablative absolute. Everything after it is a string of accusative-and-infinitive phrases — *viscera ... trahi*, *nervos ... teneri*, *membra rapi ... relinqui* — all depending on *videres*, which does not arrive until 527; the bracketed “you would see” supplies it here rather than leaving the English hanging. *partim ... partim* divides the limbs between two fates. *viva* with *viscera* is the hard word of the passage: he is alive while this happens, and the breath does not leave until 528. *in stipe* is the ablative the edition prints for the same stump it called *stipitis* at 523; the ordinary ablative of *stipes* is *stipite*, and the shorter form is left as printed.

sentences.l: you would see the broken bones give a heavy sound, and the weary breath breathed out, and that there were no parts in the body that you could recognise;
sentences.i: you would see the broken bones give out a heavy sound, the exhausted breath go out of me, and that no part of my body was left that you could recognise;
sentences.n: *videres* and *posses* are imperfect subjunctives of the indefinite second person — “you would see”, “you could” — which pull the listener up against the body. *fessamque* is the next-to-last word of 527 and its noun *animam* the second word of 528, so the adjective waits a line for its noun. *nullas ... partes* continues the same accusative series with *esse* understood, which is why the literal turns to “that there were”.

sentences.t: unumque erat omnia vulnus.
sentences.l: and the whole was one single wound.
sentences.i: and all of him was one single wound.
sentences.n: *omnia*, neuter plural, is the subject — “all his parts” — but *erat* is singular, drawn to the predicate *unum ... vulnus*. The clash of number is the whole point of the line: many parts, one wound.

sentences.t:
Num potes aut audes cladi componere nostrae,
nympha, tuam?
sentences.l: Can you, or do you dare, set your own beside our disaster, nymph?
sentences.i: Are you able — do you even dare — to set yours beside my disaster, nymph?
sentences.n: *num* introduces a question expecting the answer “no”. *componere* takes the dative of the thing compared to, *cladi ... nostrae*. *tuam* is feminine accusative with *cladem* to be supplied from *cladi*. *nostrae* is the plural used of himself alone, which is why the literal says “our” and the idiomatic “my”.

sentences.t:
Vidi quoque luce carentia regna
et lacerum fovi Phlegethontide corpus in unda,
nec nisi Apollineae valido medicamine prolis
reddita vita foret;
sentences.l: I have seen too the realms that lack the light, and I tended my mangled body in the Phlegethontian wave, and life would not have been given back except by the powerful remedy of Apollo's offspring;
sentences.i: I have seen the realms without light as well, and bathed my torn body in the water of Phlegethon; and my life would never have been restored but for the strong medicine of Apollo's offspring;
sentences.n: *quoque* here is the plain adverb “also”; it is worth checking each time, since the same letters can be *quō-que*, “and with which”. *carentia* takes the ablative *luce*, “lacking the light”. *fovi* is “warmed, soothed, tended”, the verb for caring for a wound; with *in unda* it comes close to “bathed”, which is what the idiomatic says. *Phlegethontide* is a Greek feminine adjective agreeing with *unda*. *reddita ... foret* stands for *reddita esset*, a pluperfect subjunctive in a clause contrary to fact. *Apollineae ... prolis* names the healer only as Apollo's offspring; he is not named in these lines.

sentences.t:
quam postquam fortibus herbis
atque ope Paeonia Dite indignante recepi,
tum mihi, ne praesens augerem muneris huius
invidiam, densas obiecit Cynthia nubes,
sentences.l: and when I had recovered it by strong herbs and by Paeonian aid, with Dis indignant, then Cynthia cast dense clouds before me, so that I might not, by being there in person, increase the ill-will at this gift,
sentences.i: and when I had got it back by potent herbs and healing art, to the indignation of Dis, Cynthia then threw thick clouds about me, so that my being there in person should not add to the resentment at this gift,
sentences.n: *quam* opens the clause as a connecting relative, “and this life”. *Dite indignante* is an ablative absolute, and it is doing real work: the lord of the dead has been robbed. *ope Paeonia*, “with Paeonian aid”, means the healer's art. *ne ... augerem* is a negative purpose clause, and *praesens*, “present in person”, is predicative within it. *muneris huius invidiam* is an objective genitive, the ill-will directed at the gift. *Cynthia* is the same goddess called *Dianae* at 489 and *soror Phoebi* at 550.

sentences.t:
utque forem tutus possemque impune videri,
addidit aetatem nec cognoscenda reliquit
ora mihi Cretenque diu dubitavit habendam
traderet an Delon:
sentences.l: and, so that I might be safe and could be seen without harm, she added years and did not leave my face such as could be recognised, and long she wavered whether to hand over Crete for me to have, or Delos:
sentences.i: and, so that I should be safe and could be seen without danger, she made me older and left my face unrecognisable, and for a long time she hesitated whether to hand me Crete to live in, or Delos:
sentences.n: *forem* stands for *essem*. *cognoscenda* is a gerundive used predicatively with *reliquit*: she did not leave the face as something that could be recognised. *habendam* is a second gerundive, agreeing with *Creten*, “to be had”. *Creten* and *Delon* are Greek accusatives. *dubitavit ... traderet an Delon* is an indirect deliberative question in which the first limb carries no interrogative particle at all and only *an* marks the second.

sentences.t:
Delo Creteque relictis
hic posuit nomenque simul, quod possit equorum
admonuisse, iubet deponere, “qui” que “fuisti
Hippolytus” dixit, “nunc idem Virbius esto!”
sentences.l: and, Delos and Crete set aside, she placed me here, and at the same time she bids me lay aside my name, which could put one in mind of horses, and “you who were Hippolytus,” she said, “now, the same man, be Virbius!”
sentences.i: and so, leaving Delos and Crete aside, she set me here; and at the same time she orders me to put off my name, which might put one in mind of horses, and “you who were Hippolytus,” she said, “be now the same man under the name Virbius!”
sentences.n: *Delo Creteque relictis* is one more ablative absolute. The perfect *posuit* gives way at once to the present *iubet*. The name *Hippolytus* carries the Greek word for horse, which is what *quod possit equorum admonuisse*, “which could put one in mind of horses”, is pointing at. *esto* is the future imperative, “be, from now on”. In this edition the quotation is broken so that the enclitic *que* of *quique* falls outside the quotation marks, printed as “qui” que; it is left as found.

sentences.t:
Hoc nemus inde colo, de disque minoribus unus
numine sub dominae lateo atque accenseor illi.”
sentences.l: This grove I have dwelt in ever since, and, one out of the lesser gods, I lie hidden beneath my mistress's divine power and am reckoned to her following.”
sentences.i: Ever since, I have kept this grove, and, one of the lesser gods, I stay hidden under my mistress's power and am counted in her train.”
sentences.n: *inde* is “from that time on”, and the present *colo* covers the whole stretch since. *de disque minoribus unus* uses *de* with the ablative for the partitive, “one out of the lesser gods”. In *numine sub dominae* the preposition stands after the noun it governs, *numine*, with the genitive *dominae* trailing after it. *accenseor* is “I am enrolled in addition”, with *illi* dative, “to her”. The closing quotation mark ends the speech Hippolytus began at 493.

sentences.t:
Non tamen Egeriae luctus aliena levare
damna valent,
sentences.l: Yet another's losses have no power to lighten Egeria's mourning,
sentences.i: Yet the misfortunes of another cannot lighten Egeria's grief,
sentences.n: The subject is *aliena ... damna*, neuter plural with the plural *valent*; *luctus* is accusative, the object of *levare*. *valere* with the infinitive is “to have strength to”. Egeria is named here for the first time in this part: she was *coniunx* at 487 and *nympha* at 531.

sentences.t:
montisque iacens radicibus imis
liquitur in lacrimas, donec pietate dolentis
mota soror Phoebi gelidum de corpore fontem
fecit et aeternas artus tenuavit in undas.
sentences.l: and lying at the lowest roots of the mountain she melts away into tears, until the sister of Phoebus, moved by the devotion of the grieving woman, made a cold spring out of her body and drew her limbs out thin into everlasting waters.
sentences.i: and lying at the mountain's lowest roots she dissolves into tears, until Phoebus's sister, moved by the grieving woman's devotion, made a cold spring out of her body and drew her limbs out thin into everlasting water.
sentences.n: *liquitur* is present, from *liquor*, “melt away, dissolve”; the tense turns to the perfects *fecit* and *tenuavit* only for the transformation itself, so the grief goes on and the change is done once. *dolentis* is a participle used as a noun in the genitive, “of the grieving woman”. *soror Phoebi* is the same goddess called *Dianae* at 489 and *Cynthia* at 537. *tenuavit ... in undas* is literally “thinned her limbs away into waters”.
